newsitem.title: USA: Muni, corporate bond defaults drop in 1996 - BIA.
newsitem.headline: Muni, corporate bond defaults drop in 1996 - BIA.

text.p: Bond defaults decreasd sharply in 1996 in the municipal and corporate sectors, Bond Investors Association said Friday in its annual survey.
In the municipal sector, the dollar volume for defaulted bonds showed an especially dramatic drop, association president Richard Lehman said.
Sixty-four municipal issues totalling $809 million defaulted in 1996, down from 97 issues totalling $2.36 billion in 1995, according to the report by the Miami Lakes group that tracks bond defaults.
However, the lead time for default information can be as long as six months, so final totals for 1996 could rise, Lehman said.
As in previous years, multifamily housing bonds had the highest default rate among municipals, with 24 issues going belly up, or more than one third of the total.
Special assessment district bonds and manufacturing facility bonds tied for second with 10 defaults each.
As in the past several years, California had the most municipal defaults with 23. Alabama and Colorado tied for second with four each.

The biggest municipal defaults in 1996 were two issues guaranteed by the Big River Electric Corp, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy reorganization on Sept 25, 1996. The bonds are backed by letters of credit, however, so bondholders are not expected to incur losses, Lehman's report said.

The corporate default rate dropped to 1.7 percent in 1996, a level not seen in a decade, Lehman said. Twenty-three corporte issues totalling $5.252 billion defaulted in 1996, compared with 51 issues totalling $8.245 billion in 1995.

"With the stock market at an all-time high and default rates at an historic low, it makes us wonder how long this Goldie Locks scenario, everything just right, can continue," Lehman said. "An increase in interest rates just might cool off the stock markets but it may also be the stimulus that causes default rates to return to their normal levels."
Ten-year U.S. Treasury yields were up about 50 basis points on the year while junk bond yields were down about 50 basis points, Lehman said.
"This compression of yield spreads should turn around once default rates pick up," he said.

With corporate default rates under 2 percent, "This means a mere return to to historical default rates of about 5 percent requires a doubling of current defaults. While this in and of itself is a return to normalcy, the possibility exists that a return to normalcy would cause investors to require a higher risk premium and thus cause a steepening of the quality yield curve.
"This could accelerate suddenly if banks restrict the credit available to the marginally solvent companies, thereby perpetuating a sudden wave of defaults," Lehman said.
